Because the interaction was significant, the simple effects of dose within each level of therapy were examined (Bonferroni-adjusted): CBT, F(1, 20) = 41.08, p < .001; Waitlist, F(1, 20) = 3.62, p = .143.

blocks.html: Type III sums of squares, the default in SPSS and JASP. The design is balanced (equal cell sizes), so every sums-of-squares type gives the same answer. The interaction is significant: read the main effects with care, because the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. Look at the cell means and test simple effects before you interpret a main effect alone.
Effect of dose at each level of therapy
Effect of therapy at each level of dose

Simple effects use the error term of the whole design (MSE = 2.30, df = 20). The Bonferroni column multiplies each p by the number of tests in its table. They show where a difference lives; they do not say which pairs of groups differ when a factor has three or more levels.
Equal spread (Brown-Forsythe): F(3, 20) = 14.14, p < .001.

No Shapiro-Wilk p is below .05, so nothing here argues against normality. That is weaker evidence than it sounds when groups are small. The spreads differ (p below .05). Welch t and Welch ANOVA with Games-Howell already allow for that; the classic Student t and one-way ANOVA do not.

cases.apa: A 2 × 3 between-subjects ANOVA on score showed that the main effect of therapy was significant, F(1, 25) = 9.34, p = .005, ηp² = .272; the main effect of dose was significant, F(2, 25) = 8.58, p = .001, ηp² = .407; the interaction between therapy and dose was not significant, F(2, 25) = 0.42, p = .665, ηp² = .032. For dose, Tukey comparisons of estimated marginal means gave: Low vs Mid (p = .835); Low vs High (p = .002); Mid vs High (p = .007).

blocks.html: Type III sums of squares, the default in SPSS and JASP. The cell sizes are unequal, so the sums-of-squares type matters. SPSS and JASP use Type III, which is what is shown; R's anova() uses Type I and will differ.
Pairwise comparisons of dose (Tukey)

Differences between estimated marginal means of dose (each level's mean averaged over the cell means of therapy), using the design's error term (MSE = 5.10, df = 25) and the Tukey-Kramer adjustment for unequal cell sizes. Run these only because the main effect is significant and the interaction is not.
Equal spread (Brown-Forsythe): F(5, 25) = 0.19, p = .965.

No Shapiro-Wilk p is below .05, so nothing here argues against normality. That is weaker evidence than it sounds when groups are small. No sign of unequal spread, but with a group under 10 people this test almost never fires, even when the spreads differ a lot. Compare the SDs in the table yourself.
